I should like to see our government continue the acreage bonus payments. I think this has been one of the fairest applications of government help for the purpose of meeting the cost-price squeeze that we know exists in the farming industry. It has been greatly appreciated by the farmers in my riding. There may have to be some modifications as to the administration of it so that any particular discrepancies we find now existing could be removed. But in lieu of a straight domestic two-price system which I have advocated on a previous occasion, I think this is a very effective piece of legislation and that it should be continued.
There is one other problem that affects my particular area of Saskatchewan. It has been referred to by others and I have referred to it myself previously. I have reference to the invasion of the boundary areas of Canada by United States farmers from the Dakotas and Montana. I am personally at a loss to know what is the answer to this particular problem. I think it will bear study by several departments-possibly the Department of National Revenue, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and the Department of Agriculture-in order to see what steps may be taken to make sure that these people coming into Canada would take a more serious part in the economy of the particular areas into which they come. We find that this invasion by United States' farmers has been the result of the agricultural policy in the United States of subsidizing the farmers there through the soil bank, taking large areas out of wheat production and putting them into grass. We find that these farmers in the Dakotas and in Montana, being good farmers and having large amounts invested in machinery, hate to see it lying around idle. Immediately they look for some area where they can put their machinery, ingenuity and so on to work again and get back into agriculture. They therefore migrate across into Canada and either lease or purchase land. In most cases they lease it because they feel that their own agricultural policy at home may be only temporary. They lease large amounts of Canadian farm land that some of our own Saskatchewan and Canadian farmers themselves would be greatly interested in either buying or leasing. In other words, with the capital they have available from the soil bank they are providing fairly strong competition. In some cases it is increasing the value of the land. In a few cases the Canadian farmers feel that it is making it almost prohibitive for them to compete.
The situation has a few other interesting aspects. One is that in many cases the

Americans who are coming over here are producing registered seed and are taking it back across the line with them to sell. This is something which does not aggravate the over-all wheat surplus particularly. In other cases municipal authorities, where some of this marginal area land has been put back into production, find that their tax revenues are up. But by and large quite an opposition is being developed on the part of our Canadian farmers. In order to stay in the agricultural industry those farmers who want to fit into this agrarian change to the larger economic unit especially those who have sons, feel that they should have access to this Canadian farm land rather than that it should be taken by groups coming in from the south.
As I say, I am not just too sure what the answer is to the problem, but I think several departments of government could give it very serious consideration. If our American friends should come in-and we naturally call them our American friends because we work with them on a very friendly basis apart from this matter-I personally feel that they should be encouraged possibly to come in here as landed immigrants and become permanent residents if they are going to take over this land in competition with our Canadian farmers.
In my closing remarks I should just like to say this with regard to wheat quotas. I have watched them fairly closely in our part of Saskatchewan. It happens that geographically we are about equidistant from the port of Churchill, the Pacific coast and the great lakes. When there is a demand for a certain type of grain from European countries I find that the wheat board themselves, in order to meet this demand quickly, have reached out and have drawn the grain from the closest areas adjacent to some of these ports. As a result there has been a big rectangular area, which includes my riding and some areas to the north and west, that has not had its fair share of the quota allocations. I should just like to mention this matter again. It is, of course, a matter of wheat board supervision of quotas. However, I think it is something that should be watched very closely.
We find that our farm population are very jealous with regard to their rights to equal distribution of these quotas, and rightfully so. As you know, Mr. Chairman, we get a quota of only up to about six bushels or seven bushels annually. In many cases, this does not take a great deal of the grain out of the area. As a result, in order to meet the demand of the agricultural economy now, our population in these areas wish to see that these quotas are watched closely.

With these remarks I shall conclude for the moment my observations on the agricultural estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I was very interested in the remarks of the previous speaker. I noted that at the opening of his remarks he was rather political in what he had to say. He regretted-and I use his own words-that the Saskatchewan government appeared most reluctant to co-operate in the legislation dealing with crop insurance. He also announced with considerable flourish that in Manitoba this was working very effectively indeed.
I believe that no province has yet had any experience with crop insurance and I do not completely appreciate how he can depreciate his own province in comparison with another when we consider that no province has yet had any real experience with crop insurance.
As I understand it, the Saskatchewan government is most reluctant regarding this scheme because of the heavy costs that have to be borne by the provincial government and the individual farmers concerned. In my opinion Saskatchewan is doing nothing less than its duty, and that is to protect the interests of the provincial treasury and the interests of the individual farmers concerned.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre also expressed the opinion that those engaged in agriculture in his constituency were very, very pleased-and these were his words-with existing legislation in connection with agriculture. I believe the hon. member should get outside the bounds of the city of Moose Jaw and visit a number of farmers in his riding. I believe that if he talked to the rank and file of the farmers of his riding he would feel that they were anything but very, very pleased with legislation concerning agricultural matters as it affects them.
Before we carry item 1, which is the main item and involves the salary of the minister, I should like the minister to explain to the committee and the nation why we cannot have parity prices for Canadian agriculture. Why cannot Canadian farmers who are producing those things that are consumed within Canada have the same rights as organized labour to sit across the bargaining table, perhaps with the Canadian association of consumers and the government acting as referee, and determine a price level in order to give them parity of income with all other workers of our nation?
I know this condition prevails wherever Canadian agriculture is adequately organized. This particular condition prevails in most of the major urban areas of Canada for our milk producers who market in those areas.

We have milk boards in most of the major cities of Canada; we have milk boards in most of the provinces of Canada, and when the milk producers feel they are not getting a fair deal they argue their case of rising costs or otherwise before the milk board and obtain a certain degree of equity.
Why cannot all segments of agriculture be organized in a similar way? What is the government going to do in order to help other segments of Canadian agriculture obtain at least the limited amount of equity that Canadian producers of fluid milk in the urban markets have obtained for themselves in most of our major metropolitan areas?
Our wheat farmers have a long history in this connection. I believe their history is some 80 years in length; 80 long years of organization, fighting and bitter struggle. Our wheat farmers have at least obtained orderly marketing in Canada. Why cannot other agricultural producers obtain an equal amount of equity? Why can we not have parity prices for those products that are consumed within Canada, and deficiency payments for those products that must be exported?
I see nothing wrong with the two price system for wheat. I see nothing wrong with Canadian producers of wheat being granted equity in connection with wheat consumed within Canada, and in order to give them parity of income why should they not be granted deficiency payments because of the fact that world prices may be lower than called for by parity of income calls?
I hope the minister will explain why the government has deserted and, I regret to say, persuaded many leading agricultural spokesmen of Canada to desert the basic principle of parity of income for Canadian agriculture. I am heartbroken when I have to attend a meeting of organized agriculture and realize that organized agriculture takes a penny today rather than a pound tomorrow and bows down to political expediency rather than obtaining equity and a fair, square deal. Organized agriculture kowtows to political partisanship rather than insisting on the fundamental and basic rights of the man who tills the soil.
If we can have parity of income for the fluid milk producers of Canada-and I hope we are getting near to having this for the wheat producers of Canada-why can we not have it for the potato grower, for the small fruit grower and the tree fruit grower? Why must potatoes be imported into Canada when we are able to produce potatoes at an economical price? This reflects a lack of planning and of organization. Why should strawberries be dumped on our market to the ruin of our own berry producers?

Mention has been made of the family farm.
I indicated earlier my opinion that an efficient family farm is not a farm of 18 acres with a couple of cows, a couple of laying hens, a couple of acres of wheat and a couple of sows. I support the efficient family farm, but this government is doing nothing whatever to support such a farm when it introduces legislation which would support a farm which would have 500 laying hens. The minister knows enough about modern agriculture to realize that an economic family farm unit is not constituted by 500 laying hens. If he limits his guarantees to that, all he is doing is subsidizing the inefficient agricultural producers of Canada and helping to prolong the agony of such farm families. We maintain that the efficient family farm should be a farm unit where husband, wife and family are able to recover their cash outlay plus a reasonable percentage of their investment and, in addition, receive an income on a par with that of the ordinary Canadian citizen. This cannot be accomplished by a policy of curtailing production, and I hope the minister will not follow the example of his predecessor who used to march around the country telling farmers: if you want a fair price you have to produce less. The former minister of agriculture was as ill-advised then as he is now in his new role as an advocate of nuclear weapons. The conception of restricting production in order to maintain prices is an outmoded capitalistic idea which even capitalists will no longer buy. However, the Minister of National Defence, when he was minister of agriculture, bought that concept. What an inhuman and unrealistic attitude that is, and what a typically Tory attitude it represents. The present Minister of Agriculture, unlike his predecessor, is a native of Saskatchewan and I know he has a little bit of the progressive in him. The words "Progressive Conservative" are not entirely inapplicable to him, and I hope he will not pursue the policy of his predecessor and advise all kinds of organizations across the nation that if they want a fair and equitable deal they must produce less, create scarcity, and thereby obtain better returns per unit.
I was very interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River. I should like to remind him that the wheat growers of Canada are organized. Even though I sometimes may have to disagree with what they advocate, they have come a long way over many long years. They have made sacrifices, and other branches of Canadian agriculture have not even begun to realize the potentialities of organization. I hope the minister will supply some leadership to these other branches of agriculture in order to help them to help themselves to get a fair deal. We have

often heard of lobbying legislators. I know of no group in all Canadian history, outside the investment dealers, the Canadian chamber of commerce and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, who have lobbied more effectively in this House of Commons than have the wheat growers of Canada. I should like to see the day when the onion growers, the potato growers, the tomato growers and the poultry farmers are organized to the point when they can make their unified voices heard, and I hope, as I said, that the minister will supply some leadership so as to enable these people, who together outnumber the wheat growers by far, to obtain equity on the national scene.
Much has been made in speeches of the minister's "trees galore" plan. I admire the plan. I think it is wonderful. I think it is good. However, it will do very little to help the farmers of Canada in either the minister's lifetime or my own. This is a long range program which the minister is advocating and there are matters of much greater urgency to be attended to now.
The hon. member for Moose Mountain had some good words to say about the minister but his words of praise also included the minister's parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Provencher and that, I think, was an error. The hon. member for Provencher, as I understand it, is in favour of the factory farm. We in this group and I think I can speak for my colleagues-are in favour of the family farm as opposed to the factory farm.
The hon. member also mentioned the problem of unemployment insurance for farm workers. I agree that they should be covered by unemployment insurance. However, what is basically needed is to give to the farmers an adequate income so that they can afford to pay a proper wage to their help. If they can pay an adequate wage they will be able to get the help. I realize the farmer is unable to do so because he does not get fair treatment. He is unable to pay the wages that industrial firms are able to pay, and therefore very often is unable to get the help he needs. Unemployment insurance will not provide the answer even though it ought to be introduced and made applicable to farm workers. But that is not the real problem; the real problem is to give the farmer enough net income so that he can pay his employees a wage which would make the position attractive and the wages comparable to those which are paid in industry today.

Before the item carries I would like to ask the minister a question. Is the federal government planning to introduce legislation which will permit the federal government to co-operate with the provinces to

pay compensation to farmers whose animals are destroyed because of rabies? I understand that some time ago there was an outbreak of rabies in various provinces in Canada and by order in council compensation was paid on the basis of the federal, provincial and municipal governments co-operating. Since then in my own particular area one or two animals have died and no compensation has been forthcoming. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that this is unjust. Simply because no epidemic is raging at the particular time certain people suffer losses, they should not be denied compensation. Farmers are quite co-operative with the federal Department of Agriculture. Indeed, they are quite enthusiastic about the help they receive. I think it would build up confidence on the part of the farmers if such legislation were forthcoming. Will the minister inform the committee in the course of his reply.

Before the item carries, and since I do not think it would be appropriate on any other item, I wish to put one or two queries to the minister to give him the opportunity to explain to us what is happening with respect to the view of one correspondent who described the minister as doing political farming. Perhaps I can make my point clear by reading this piece from the Victoria Daily Times of January 17, by a very distinguished member of the press gallery, Mr. Tom Gould, which is entitled "Political Farming":
Agriculture Minister Alvin Hamilton has a decided advantage over opposition critics of the government's farm program. Since taking over the agriculture portfolio, the minister has discovered a way of using the taxpayer's own money to distribute what amounts to political propaganda. The information division of the department has for a number of years been producing a twice-monthly publication entitled "Farm News", that is sent to every newspaper and radio station in Canada. In the past, ministers left it alone. It was a purely departmental publication, dealing in matters of concern to Canada's farming population.
It carried articles on the control of wild oats, on the use of chemical fertilizers, and a wide range of problems studied by the labs and experimental farms operated by the government.
Mr. Hamilton has decided to take advantage of this publication to spread the government's views on agriculture. He made his debut as a columnist in the current issue, on the highly-controversial subject of allowing feed mills to purchase grain directly from producers without first obtaining delivery quotas from the Canadian wheat board.
The column bears his picture, and is titled: "The Minister Reports."
Officials of the information division have been informed that the minister intends providing them with a similar column once a month to start, and may step it up to twice-a-month to make sure he gets in every issue. His first effort takes up one sixth of the print space in the current issue.
It is an out-and-out defence of the government's action in the feed mills controversy, and a denial of the claims made by critics of the action.
People close to Mr. Hamilton say the use of what was a purely departmental information outlet is

Mr. Hamilton obviously plans to spend far more time out on the road, convincing farmers they have never had it better, than in sitting in Ottawa running the department. He has made a dozen major policy speeches.

-and they want to retain that hold in the next federal election.

Mr. Halliwell has obtained leave of absence from his newspaper.

member lor Burnaby-Coquitlam. I do not believe the minister is a native of Saskatchewan any more than I am. I understand he was born in that little farming settlement of Kenora, Ontario.
I saw him there in 1938.

He has been in Saskatchewan quite a long time, just as some others who were not actually born on the western prairies have spent a lot of time there. The Russell newspaper, the Banner, in its issue of February 23, contained this article under the heading "Selling Mr. Hamilton". I do not suppose it was really suggested that there was any reintroduction of slavery; I suppose they were using the word "selling" in that modern sense of Madison avenue and not in the old-fashioned sense of the Louisiana slave market. I quote:
Surpluses would soon vanish if the federal minister of agriculture put as much effort into selling farm produce as he does in selling Mr. Hamilton to the public. As though he didn't get enough press releases from various government departments, Mr. Hamilton has hired himself a special editorial writer to build up an efficient, high pressure and extensive public relations and information service. And we in the newspaper field are feeling the effects already, for there is hardly a mail coming in without one or more releases from his information service, which often include a text of one of his speeches. All have that stereotype beginning "Agricultural Minister Alvin Hamilton said today." One would need a fair sized daily to relay all the material to the public. Offhand, we would say that 25 mimeographed pages are received each week and multiply this by some 800 weeklies in Canada, as well as dailies, radio and T.V. stations, and you have a lot of paper. No wonder we all have such big waste paper baskets.
Perhaps that would explain the minister's new policy on planting trees. If this proliferation of press releases is going to continue at the rate that, according to these writers, it has already reached since he became minister, he may feel that the existing crop of spruce trees in the country will not produce enough paper for all his press releases and therefore we must increase the production of wood in order to produce the necessary paper and thereby produce a crop that will not be in surplus.
The minister was not here, of course, but I remember the days when the minister's friends were over here where I am now and there was no theme on which Mr. Drew, the former leader of the party, and other members spent more time than the extravagance of the previous Liberal government in its information services in the various departments. Promises were made in those days that when the Conservatives came into office they would fire all these publicity people, get down to the business of dealing with the problems of the country and let their solution of the problems speak for itself.

That does not seem to have been the practice that has been followed in many departments but I do not think there is any department where there has been such a conspicuous increase in the crop as in the minister's department where, notwithstanding some of the other undisposable surpluses, I have no doubt that from the look of things it will not be too long until the biggest agricultural surplus will be the surplus of the minister's press releases and other propaganda of one kind and another. Apart from any harvest of votes the minister expects to get out of these press releases, which is hardly a legitimate expenditure of the funds of the Department of Agriculture, it did seem to me that he should explain to the committee precisely what advantage he thinks the farmers get from seeing his picture in this information bulletin which, according to this story, was formerly a compilation of technical information of one sort and another.
I think he should explain just what justification there is for this proliferation of propaganda and expenditure because it does seem to me that we have enough real problems that should engage the full time and attention of ministers instead of their indulging in this practice of building up huge propaganda machines with the avowed purpose or at any rate the apparent purpose- perhaps the minister would not avow it-of political self-glorification. I felt that perhaps the minister had been so busy issuing these things, so busy making these speeches and had spent so much time on the road that he had not had much time to read the newspapers to see what kind of reception his road show was getting and that perhaps it would be helpful to him if this were drawn to his attention. Mr. Chairman, is the minister prepared, if he has not already done so, to amplify the indication he gave earlier in the session that he was giving serious consideration to bringing pulpwood under the Agricultural Stabilization Act or some form of legislation that would give a better price to the settlers or farmers for whom pulpwood is becoming increasingly a very large source of income?

Mr. Chairman, several questions have been posed. The Agricultural Stabilization Act was one of the first major efforts under the government's agricultural development program to get at one of the fundamental weaknesses in agriculture, namely, the rise and fall in prices.

The act covers some 17 products and with respect to most of these products it seems to be working quite well. From listening to various hon. members and having in mind the way the act is working it is obvious it is not entirely satisfactory in relation to hogs and eggs. I think the fundamental reason for this is that as a result of the plentiful supplies of feed, particularly in western Canada, it has been and is so easy to expand the production of these two items. Any slight adjustment upwards in price immediately attracts tremendous production and a surplus situation.
On several occasions I have indicated that I, personally, am not completely satisfied with the way the stabilization act has worked out with regard to these two products. I would suggest that if I have been honest in saying that, then other hon. members could be equally honest by searching their own consciences, and calculating the known effects of their suggestions on economic production in this country, before they make suggestions which have not been thoroughly thought out. If the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska is suggesting that western farmers receive a price for eggs comparable to that received by Quebec farmers, his suggestion would be very well received by western farmers. However, the majority of western farmers are aware that, with their ability to produce cheap feed, they can produce eggs or hogs in unlimited quantities at prices with which the eastern farmer could not compete. If the western farmer did this, then not only would he destroy the price for himself but for all producers of eggs and hogs in Canada. I think producers generally owe the western farmer a great deal because of his restraint in not rushing into the production of these two products.
I should like also to sound a small warning to the eastern producers of products for which prices are not as high as they are in the west. I am referring particularly to sugar beets. If the sugar beet producer in eastern Canada were to ask for a price comparable to that received in western Canada, the result would be a great increase in the production of sugar beets. This, in turn, would destroy the market for the western producer. We have to realize, therefore, that in this country the basic economic rules should continue to apply. Meanwhile, as I said earlier, I do not believe the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska really implies that we should have the same price for these products all across Canada. If he is implying that there should be a regional price, and regional supports, then of course that is something different. I believe that is a suggestion worthy of consideration.

The hon. member for Port Arthur asked about bringing pulpwood under the stabilization act. I think this will eventually come about. However, some time has to pass before there will be active tree growing operations on farms. We are very pleased to see the promotion, through farm associations, of the movement to have trees on farms. I intend to encourage this in every way possible. I believe a good deal of time must elapse yet before we get to the stage of putting pulpwood under the stabilization act. I do not want anyone to get the idea I am opposed to putting pulpwood under the act because, eventually, I think this will happen. If our program under the other legislation is going to be successful, then within a year or two we will have to begin working out some kind of formula for giving to those who are producing trees the protection of the stabilization act.
In so far as the tree industry is concerned, I think the preliminary step will have to be a marketing board set-up or some arrangement whereby the farmers get into an organization to protect themselves. The hon. member for Fraser Valley mentioned the need for advertising butter. No person could agree with him more than I do. We have one item in the estimates for advertising. I believe it is about $200,000, which is not nearly enough to compete with the advertising of the big corporations. I think the producers will have to consider enlarging their advertising program and instead of setting aside an amount each June for this purpose they will have to do so on a monthly basis.

The minister has said he looks forward to bringing pulpwood under this act. I should like to suggest to him that some effort be made under his rural rehabilitation program which he hopes to put through the house this year, to switch marginal areas to the production of wood. I cannot think of a better incentive to get more farmers interested in the production of wood than the knowledge that they will get a fair price

for their pulpwood. Despite the inquiry into pulpwood prices in eastern Canada, and despite the penalties that were incurred by the companies for contravention of the combines act, it seems to me that there is no real indication pulpwood prices are a great deal better in the province of Quebec. I think there is a real indication that prices are better because of the action taken by the provincial government to set up marketing boards.
I think perhaps hon. members know, especially the hon. member for Cochrane, that in Ontario there is legislation under which marketing boards for pulpwood could be set up. However, the provincial government will not give any lead in this respect. I have a communication from the minister of agriculture to the effect that he has no intention of encouraging such a step. The department of lands and forests will not encourage it. Surely the minister must concede that marketing boards must develop within a provincial framework. In the second largest pulpwood province we have a government whose policy is diametrically opposed to the policy followed in Quebec, the other main pulpwood producing province. We need some way of resolving this difference in order to arrive at a uniform framework.
Can the minister suggest to us how Ontario could be brought to the stage of establishing some rudimentary marketing organization? Perhaps the minister could tell us how this step could be taken and what leadership his department could give in achieving this development. I should like him to suggest to me what kind of regional set-up would be evolved for pricing if we had pulpwood under this stabilization act. It is quite obvious that the price of pulpwood in Sault Ste. Marie is quite likely to be lower than the price of pulpwood in Port Arthur because in Port Arthur there are more mills competing. It is quite likely that pulpwood prices in Ottawa are almost certain to be lower than in areas where there are very few settlers and very few farmers such as up in northwestern Ontario. Can he suggest to us how he sees this act working in view of these regional differences, and in view of the fact that the province of Ontario has given no lead at all in establishing marketing boards?

I have not too much to add to what I have already said. It is a subject on which I have put some considerable thought. However, this is not a problem upon which I wish to elucidate at the present time. We have made great strides in the last few years. Quebec has set up marketing boards for pulpwood production, and this has resulted in increased prices. I

hope to have some discussions with the provinces in the not too distant future, and this is one subject we will be discussing. We, on this side, have some hesitancy about imposing our will on the provinces. We do not believe in centralization. We do know that, at least in theory, if you are one who does not consider the powers of the provinces you can push these things upon them. However, I should like to discuss these things with the provinces and do them on a voluntary basis rather than by means of pressure techniques.

There is one last qualifying remark I should like to make in this respect. During the last election campaign the Prime Minister, I believe at Rimouski, Quebec, according to the documented record of some of his promises produced by the Liberal party, gave an indication that pulpwood was going to be brought under this particular act. It is all very well for the minister to say that he does not believe in pressuring, that he is not a centralizer nor is the government of which he is a member, that they want to go slowly, that they do not want to strain things too much. What I am afraid of is this. We are going to have another election campaign shortly. I think it would be a pity if again we had this promise dangled of pulpwood being brought under this act without any clarification as to how it could be done. The minister will remember that his predecessor-who, if I could phrase it in this way, was a bit more of a hard rock than he is-rose in his place in this house a number of times and in effect threw completely chilled water upon this whole idea. The present minister has given an indication that he has more interest in or compassion for the subject. In view of past election promises, in view of an election campaign coming and in view of the switch that he has made in the intentions of the department towards this project, I think we deserve to know more about how this department plans to bring it about.

My reason for raising this matter is that I believe, from my understanding of the legal aspects of the case, the farmer did get a fair hearing. The prosecution put forward a fair case and his lawyer received a fair hearing but my contention is that the evidence put forward at that time and the reasons established in the case were not sufficient to warrant a conviction. The conviction was obtained by the department themselves because they felt there was a need to establish this kind of precedent. To this extent I agree with the department.
We have now got into a field where we are selling cattle to countries such as Argentina for $20,000, $30,000 and $40,000 a head. If we are not in a position to establish a breed, maintain a fair and honest record of that breed and handle artificial insemination, which is a completely new field of very recent origin, we are going to be suspect when we sell our cattle to other countries.
In this relationship we have had in the last few years something that has been very detrimental to this whole process. I am
Supply-Agriculture
referring to something in the Holstein-Friesian breed that is called the red factor. The red factor did enter into this particular case. As everybody knows, a Holstein cow has certain definite characteristics. She must be black and white in colour; she must have five points that are white; her forestockings and the switch of her tail must be white before she can be registered as being of the Holstein-Friesian breed. There are also other considerations that enter into this matter.
In recent times two purebred animals have been producing a red calf which is not regis-terable under this act. This, of course, has become such a big problem in Holland, where the breed developed, that they have now set up a red register; but only very recently in Canada, within the last few months, the Holstein-Friesian association itself, and therefore I presume the Department of Agriculture through its livestock division, recognized this red factor as part of the problem. Today these livestock associations recognize that this red factor is a very real problem and now when they advertise semen they state, where it applies, that a bull carries a red factor and thus people are warned.
You may wonder, Mr. Chairman, why this is of any importance at all. Perhaps I may use an example which happened on the family farm. My brother was very pleased last summer when he was able to obtain semen from one of the best bulls in Canada, a bull worth $45,000 at the time. He bred this bull artificially to one of his cows, a cow which has an excellent record. A bull calf of this stock would normally be worth several thousand dollars, but when this particular calf was born it was a red calf which looked more like an Ayrshire than a Holstein. Anyway, it was worth $22 rather than $1,000 or $2,000 as might have been expected. Neither the government nor the Holstein-Friesian society has given much consideration to this problem until recently but I am pleased to state that the society is now giving some consideration to it and that its advertising now carries notices where necessary stating that a bull or cow is known to carry the red factor. The societies themselves are becoming increasingly aware of the difficulty and one of the units buying a bull at a very large price has stipulated in the contract that if it were proven later that the bull carried a red factor the purchase price would be greatly reduced. While that particular bull still has a favourable background and heritage, the calves produced by that bull are worth very little.
In the case about which I am concerned, the Rowe case, as far as I have been able to find out, Mrs. Rowe-and this is one of these

sad cases-decided to leave Mr. Rowe but was unable to obtain a divorce, and because she wanted to get even with her husband she went to the head of the livestock division and laid a charge that he was falsely registering certain calves. That is how the investigation began. Checking the documents provided by the department I was unable to find any information of what interviews led to the proceedings or what the contents of those interviews were. But it appears from the information which I asked to be tabled in the house that the lawyer acting for the crown did interview this woman on several occasions. I should have liked to have seen the herd book in this particular case. The herd book is a book kept by a farmer under certain regulations which require him to record the breeding dates together with the names and dates of calves born to particular animals. Farmers also keep a stable book which gives breeding dates and states whether an animal is artificially bred, to whom it was bred, the dates of the first service, the second service and so on. To date I have been unable to find such a stable book. Anyone who has any experience with dairy herds would be able after consulting the herd book and the stable book to reach a conclusion as to whether or not a farmer was keeping adequate records. Up to the present the closest thing I can find from the R.C.M.P. is that they destroyed these along with certain other documents at the end of a given period of time.
The court case itself involved a number of things which I do not think are of very much interest to this committee and which in my opinion should not have been of much interest to the department. There was a great deal of talk about whether this animal was bred six months after she had been bred the first time, about whether this was technically possible. They used such experts as Dr. Gamble and Dr. Humble and several other leading veterinarians from the Ontario Agriculture College, and they came to the conclusion that this animal could have been bred six months after it was already bred and in calf for that length of time, though this was unlikely. I think it is perfectly true that it is very unlikely that you would breed a number of cattle more than once or twice in these circumstances. In this case the farmer claims to have bred her in January and she had a calf nine months later. This calf was registered. She was bred again two months after that and she had a calf, then, nine months following that, and the second calf was registered. Now the department begins an investigation into this particular case. They question not the second calf but the first calf, and this seems to me to be the stupid part of the whole case. If this cow was bred in

January she could have had the calf, as the farmer said, the first time. If she had been bred six months after she had been bred the first time she could not possibly have a six months premature calf and therefore the second calf would not have been possible. It is not physically possible to have a three or four month premature calf in the second instance. But the department has not questioned the right of the registration of this second calf. In reading the evidence and going over it-and there are four or five hours of evidence-I see no possibility of the judge establishing the fact that this cow could have had a second calf if he did not agree with the farmer that she had had the first. The Holstein-Friesian society made a great to-do about the blood testing of cattle, as you know, Mr. Chairman, people have four or five types of blood. Mr. Chairman, this would not prove that the cow was not the dam. I think that some consideration on the part of the department should be given to this question of first, second and third services. I have some new evidence which I think should have been brought to the attention of the court.
Here is a man who bred the cow the first time. The cow was Silver Bell Root. She was bred on January 26, 1952. She carries the registration number 168534, and the tag number 5160. This cow was bred on April 23, 1952. I have also a slip here which indicates that a cow bearing this particular number was killed and sold for fox meat in March of that year. In other words, the artificial unit was breeding this cow one month after she had been sold for fox meat. This evidence is available to the department.
What I am saying about these artificial units is proven by evidence I received from a friend of mine who is a veterinarian in the Brantford area. He tells me that they now colour the semen. They put artificial colouring in because there were so many mistakes made over such a long period of time. Because of that, most of the units colour the semen so that there can be no mistake. The farmer, or the man who is doing this work, does not now mix up the semen in the test tube in his refrigerator in his home. The colour will give him some indication of which bull the semen happens to come from; therefore, he is assured that the semen he is using in the service he is giving comes from the bull he thinks it does, and the farmer is given much greater assurance that the calf which is born to the cow was sired by the bull he is paying his money for, to perform the service. If hon. members would

Supply-Agriculture
like to drop into my office at any time I would be glad to show them some pictures taken of these two cows, the mother and the daughter.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Hon. members laugh but they should give consideration to this. This purebred livestock registration is a relatively new field. When you are selling animals for $40,000 to $50,000 it is no joke, and if the importers knew how damned stupid we sometimes are in our legislation and how loose we are in our way of doing business they would not pay $30,000 or $40,000 for an animal unless they were given an assurance that they are receiving what they are paying for.
The hon. member does not know what he is talking about.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The hon. member should get up and say what he knows. I think I know a lot more than he does although I do not know him or where he comes from.
In the main, the farmers used to depend on the Holstein-Friesian association for descriptions. If you check on the back of the registration you will see there is a picture of the cow, there is a picture of the particular animal registered. The farmer draws on all the black and white markings and that is how they were registered for years, and this is still how they register them. There is a similarity in cows as there is in people. There is a similarity between mother and daughter, father and daughter, father and son, and so on. The descendants of human beings show similarities and this is true of animals also.
If hon. members will look over the pictures of these animals, which I would be happy to show them, they will see similarities. In fact, it is surprising how similar they are. The markings on the head of the cows are almost identical. If you look at the markings on the cows you will see a great similarity. It is true that this is no proof. I agree with this, but this is what the Holstein-Friesian people have depended on for years, and they still depend on it. We should not depend on this phony court case. I wonder why the department did not appeal the case? I wonder why they did not take the case to a higher court? Just why they did not I am sure I do not know.
Let hon. members laugh. The government spent a great deal of money on this court case and in my opinion they did not get a conviction that would stand up as a precedent in any other court in the country. The court in question was a small rural court of summary jurisdiction. Most of us have been in such courts. A lot of us have had
to go there because of traffic tickets and we know what kind of justice is dispensed in a great number of them. I have been there and I know what kind of justice a person gets. Maybe other hon. members have been more fortunate.
This is a serious matter, Mr. Chairman, and I should like to keep it that way. We are going to have to decide that we should give these associations all the assistance we can. We want to establish the best breeds possible and give the greatest assurance to buyers from abroad that they are getting what they are paying for. Let us not fool ourselves. We should establish these blood types. If Dr. Humble of the Ontario veterinary college has carried on his experiments to the point where, as he claims, he can ascertain 80 different factors in cattle, then we should see that this is carried on and developed to the point where we can make use of it. Let us develop some cases where we know and can prove that the dam is the dam in question. Then we can play around with the sire. If we question the dam and question the sire and cannot be sure of either the dam or the sire no specialist in this country will ever say that you can tell by blood test what particular cow or bull was the parent of the calf in question. You have to have one known parent.
I have read the evidence and many of the articles of Dr. Humble who is considered to be one of the leading experts not only in Canada but in the world and I have failed to find where they have used known bulls rather than unknown bulls. Maybe it is necessary to establish more than 14 or 15 factors and maybe it is possible that it is only necessary to establish a smaller number.
In this particular case I think that in all fairness a blood sample could have been taken from the second calf and so far as blood factors are concerned they might have found a similarity with the first calf. This would have been at least interesting and in my opinion would have established some similarity between the first calf and the second calf.
Hon. members should read the evidence and the letters exchanged because they will see that the government was pleased to get this conviction. I am sure I do not know why. If a good case had been established that could have been used as a precedent I would have thought they had accomplished something but if they only prosecuted to collect $500 from some poor farmer and to take away from him the privilege of producing purebred cattle then I am ashamed of them. If they took this action for the first reason I think they had an obligation to

bring forward the best people they could on both sides and try to establish the case.
If the Minister of Agriculture wants to do so, this case can still be given consideration. The cow is still living. The bull has been examined by Dr. Humble on two separate occasions. The blood of the second bull in question was tested but that bull is now dead, although it was not dead, as intimated by the government, at the time of the hearing. The bull was still available and was not killed until November of that year. I am quite sure he was blood tested. I am quite sure that all bulls in the artificial insemination units are being tested now. This case can still be reopened because the cow and the two calves are still available on the farm in question. It was not the farmer's obligation to establish a decent case.
I have talked to a number of veterinarians who are quite concerned about what is taking place in the breeding of cattle through artifi-' cial insemination. I am sure all hon. members will be happy to know, if they are not already aware of it, that artificial insemination has been a boon not only to Holstein-Friesian breeders but to breeders of all other types of livestock as well. It means that a farmer for a minimum amount of money can secure the services of the best sire in the field in which he is interested. For $15 or $20 he can secure the services of the best bull in any of the milk breeds, Holstein, Ayrshire or Jersey. Those who are raising the beef breeds can secure the services of bulls for about the same price. This means that the average farmer, even though he is remote from the place where these expensive bulls are located, can secure the services of an animal worth $20,000 to $30,000. This means that the department also has an obligation and responsibility to guarantee that the farmer receives what he pays for.
In this particular case, when the expert said that this calf was not the progeny of this particular mating the government should have been willing to prove that the calf produced from the cow was as a result of using the service of this artificial insemination unit, that the farmer was receiving the service for which he was paying and the protection to which I think he is entitled.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare should also be concerned about this matter because there are great implications so far as humans are concerned in light of the fact that artificial insemination is now being used in that field as well. Every effort should be made-certainly the procedure is going to have to be more exact in the case of humans-to see that there is a method of assuring the farmer that the semen he buys 90205-6-223J
Supply-Agriculture
from the artificial insemination unit is semen from the bull for whose services he is paying.
In the case in question a conviction was obtained simply on the finding that the calf was not the result of this particular mating and the silly business of breeding the cow the second time when she was six months in calf was introduced. As I see it, this was simply a red herring so far as this matter was concerned, and I think the department has been remiss in its duties. I am most concerned about this matter. My family has depended for many years on the breeding of cattle by this means. They have spent a great deal of time at the experimental farm at New Liskeard and have spent a great deal of time and money on their own farm in developing purebred cattle. In many cases we are far removed from the services of the best bulls which are found in southern Ontario. Their services are only available to us through artificial insemination. I think the case I have mentioned tonight is a disgrace to the government. It is a disgrace that they should try to establish it as a precedent in connection with purebred livestock.
I regret to inform the hon. member that his time has expired.
Mr. Chairman, I have read a lot about this case and I hope the minister is going to reply to the presentation of the hon. member for Timiskaming.

Mr. Chairman, as a past president of the Holstein association of Canada I feel I should say a word at this time. Through the press I have obtained some information about the case that has been mentioned and discussed for the last half hour. Personally I am absolutely certain that the president and the board of directors of the Holstein association are on the job for the sole purpose of breeding good cattle and keeping them pure. There is the odd case, of course, where a mistake is made but if a mistake is made that is no reason why these animals should be bred again and again. I know of lots of cases where the bull has cost $40,000 and where the cost of service has been $100 for a proven calf. I want to say here in this committee that any group of men who have been breeding Holsteins for the last 75 or 100 years would want to keep the breed pure. The way to do that is to look after the records properly, and that is what the association is doing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am pleased to hear-
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Let us not hear these gentlemer. say, "No, no". I am getting fed up with some

Supply-Agriculture
of these western members who are not interested in anything except what concerns the western farmer. They are so ready to pass the other items.
You are wasting so much time, though.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I do not care if we spend a week on this item. It is very important to the eastern farmers. I do not care whether or not the hon. member for Brome-Missis-quoi likes it. It does not interest me one iota.
What does interest us is the clarity of thought so that you do not take so much of the time of the committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You have no thought, let alone clarity.
Order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I have been pleased to hear the words of the past chairman of the Hol-stein-Friesian association. I am in complete agreement with him. Within the last 40 years, through the efforts of this association, this country has progressed from a position of having no purebred cattle to the point where out of about 130,000 registrations last year the Holstein-Friesian association had about 88,000. I think this is an excellent record. I feel that a good deal of the credit should be given to Mr. Clements and his father because the two of them have alternated in serving as secretary of this association for practically the lifetime of the association. The organization, however, has not been able to keep up with some of the faults that have appeared in it.
The past president of the organization may be interested to know that 16 or 17 registrations of Holstein cattle were discussed in this particular case. He may be interested in reading a transcript of the case, and he would find that the office of the Holstein-Friesian association in Brantford had made minor and major changes in seven or eight of these registrations. This would mean that almost one third of the cards had been changed. The best bookkeeping practices have not been followed. I agree that in many cases these changes have been made necessary because you cannot have two cows known by the same name. If they have the same surname, I suppose you would call it, then you would have to change the prefix.
I have been worried, as a result of reading the correspondence in this case, to find that the secretary of this association is very interested in getting this particular conviction. In my opinion, he was more interested in getting a conviction than in seeing that the case was really established. I do not know

who is the mother or father of this particular little calf. If this were the British parliament I suppose we could get this calf legitimized by the simple process of passing an act as was done in England for years when they wanted to legitimize some member of royalty. There was a particular act passed for this purpose. I do not believe that is our intention here. What we are trying to do is to use this particular case as a warning of the type of thing that should not happen in this country. Our little people should be protected. The farmer should be given all the protection he can be given.
I have seen this farmer's herd of cattle and, although they are not registered now, they looked like very good cows to me. I am told that at the time of the investigation this farmer had only one cow on the premises which was not a purebred animal. It would seem very odd that he would jockey these animals around within the herd when that would not do him any good. I believe this was a particularly bad case. Let us take the example of a farmer who is in the milk producing business. Why would he leave a cow for three years without breeding her, when she should be producing milk the second year? Why would he wait that length of time, unless she was showing exceptional promise and her breeding was exceptionally high? He would have disposed of her before the end of the third year. The department maintained that she did not calve until she was three years old. There is no question raised about the second calf she was supposed to have had. If she had this second calf, the calf would have been premature by four or five months.
People can laugh this off, and the minister can say this is a matter of no importance. I am not sure whether or not the present Minister of Agriculture knows about this particular case. I know the arrogant attitude of the former minister, and I can well imagine that he would not have been interested in one little farmer, particularly in eastern Canada. I do feel the government must be interested in this matter. If we have a bill of rights which means anything, then it should protect all people. I have four or five letters commending the character of this farmer. I have letters from the bank in his area, from the dairies, from the cheese factory and from the farmers in the area. They all state that he is a highly respected man there.
If this farmer believes he did not get justice, then I believe the department should bend over backwards to ascertain whether or not he did and try to clear his name. These animals are valuable. Why should I go out and have them blood tested again, just to

prove whether the department is right or wrong? The farmer thinks he has a case, and he goes to the Department of Justice where they tell him that the time for an appeal has passed but they would be happy to consider a parole of a remission in this case. This gentleman wants to establish his record again. I am not too sure why he is interested to this extent. I do feel he has been very courageous in fighting this case the length of time he has. More important even than the fact he feels he did not get justice in our courts is the fact that the experts in the Department of Agriculture, in my opinion, do not feel they have a case that will stand up in a major court of this country. Frankly, I have checked with the department and they claim they will not use this case as a precedent.
They do not give a damn.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Perhaps they do not, I am inclined to believe this is true. If it is true, they are making a hollow mockery out of the work of farmers who are interested in establishing a herd of purebred cattle. If the farmers feel the federal government is not interested or concerned in this matter, then they will be worried. This farmer has received the co-operation of the veterinary college and they are willing to supply information. If you will check the information that was given by those officials you will find that neither one of them gave evidence in this particular case that would be detrimental to the farmer. It would just as easily have established the farmer's case as it would have established the reverse. Weeks and weeks went by and pressure was brought to bear on the magistrate before a decision in this particular case was rendered. I am concerned, because, I have said we have always been interested in the increasing growth and the extension of the breeding records of our various purebred livestock in Canada.
In northern Ontario now we are seeing a great increase in the registrations of cattle both with respect to Holstein-Friesian and in the beef Friesian. This is reflecting now in the markets, in the community sales and the value for the products which the farmers themselves are getting. It is resulting in better milk production for the farmer and in increased sales. Among the farmers themselves we are now finding some with only four or five purebred cows who are willing to pay the premium price that is necessary in order to buy local purebred bulls. This was not true ten or 15 years ago. Very few farmers were interested in increasing the breed of their animals. Through the influence of Holstein-Friesian this has been extended into pigs, sheep, beef cattle and now horses. In our area there is a
Supply-Agriculture
relationship between the artificial inseminating units in the work they do, and this work in the main is of an excellent nature. They are producing and they are giving the service they are supposed to give, but there is a possibility-and it will always remain-of a slip anywhere from the time that semen is collected till it is inserted by the agent in the artificial inseminating unit. It seems to me that the government itself, if it is going to continue to work towards increasing the breed, is going to have a great deal more consideration to the matter and a great deal more assistance from the federal government in this field. Within the next five or ten years the red factor in the Holstein-Friesian breed is going to be a major problem. It is going to be a problem that I am sure is going to cost the farmers thousands and thousands of dollars as it cost my brother this year when he expects a calf worth $1,000, when it is dropped you get a calf that is worth $22.
This is being repeated with this one particular bull. One out of every three calves carried the red factor and were not eligible for registration. The problem is how to eliminate or to eradicate this situation. The answer is not known yet. It certainly has not been tested in hogs where they have developed separate registration for these particular cattle. Any assistance that the federal government can give will be of great help to the farmer. I think that one of the things the minister could do is this. Certainly he is going to have to answer these questions because if he does not do so I will raise them in a legal context next time. I will document them and will go into all the grim and gory details of this particular case. We will go into this matter if the minister cannot give us some assurance that he is interested in this problem.
Is that a filibuster threat?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I will make it a filibuster or whatever you want to call.
That is what you can call a filibuster threat.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am interested in seeing that justice is done. I will be quite happy in obtaining an explanation. If no explanation is forthcoming, then we will take other methods of obtaining one. I am no expert in this field. If I were I would probably not be here.
I can tell you this, Mr. Chairman. I can look around this building and I do not see many who can class themselves as experts on any subject. I have given some consideration to this particular case. I have read the court evidence. I have read the brief. Almost every hon. member has had the opportunity to do this. If they read it and found nothing of a

Supply-Agriculture
questionable nature in it, then they are in conflict with the newspapers that have read it and have found a great deal of conflict in it. They are in conflict with a number of people to whom I have talked privately. I think there is an obligation resting on the minister to give us some assurance that something will be done about this matter, that consideration is being given to this matter that has been raised on blood testing. The Holstein-Friesian association, in an article in their magazine, brags of the fact that they were able to establish this case, that now they had a precedent that was established and would continue for all times. In my opinion there was no precedent; there was a very weak case and at a very low level of court. It seems to me-
Order. The Chair has been quite lenient with the hon. member in reference to the courts. I think that he must obey section 152 under which no slighting reference to the courts may be made.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am surprised that this matter always arises, that even if you prove they are wrong, you have not the right to do so. This may be true. However, I will certainly abide by Your Honour's decision on that matter. I am concerned about this matter. If the minister has not studied the case, I would be happy if he would study it and would give us a reply at a later date. I am quite happy to take his word that he will do this. I feel that it is a rather complicated field, and one in which he would have the advice of people like Dr. Gamble and Dr. Humble, world renowned specialists in this field, that he would have the advantage of the experience they have had. If he gave consideration to this matter or if he were to direct his officials to do so, they might come up with a different conclusion in this particular case; and while it is much more important they might come to a conclusion that would allow a much better method of policing the Live Stock Pedigree Act itself.
As I have said, if we are going to be in the export market, we shall also be in the import market. We shall eventually find that our .artificial inseminating units are buying cattle from Holland, England and other countries, the same as they have bought horses or purebred sires from Belgium and Percherons from other countries and eventually we are going to have to use this blood testing to establish .an international record. They are going to have to have enough known factors. This only proves a negative; it does not prove a positive. However, it proves a negative. If we know definitely and have methods of knowing through control of artificial inseminating units -and we use no control over them now either
from the federal government or elsewhere- once we know this, then we shall be able to question the farmer on the dam of that animal. We shall be able to say that we know the sire was particular animal and that these are the factors in the blood of that sire. But at the present time we are taking the word of four or five different people, including the veterinarian who takes the semen, the man who handles it in the laboratory, and they are all put into the laboratory at the same time and there is a great deal of opportunity for a mix-up there. Then there is the shipping and the handling through the transportation and then again the man who travels through the farming area handling the semen at that end. Until the government is in a position to guarantee the sire, how are we going to breed, for instance, a mare in this country to a purebred Belgian stallion in Belgium if we are not going to be able to prove at a later date that the sire of that mating is from that particular mating if the question arises?
We will not be dealing with small figures in this connection. These purebred animals which are used primarily for breeding purposes cost $20,000 or $30,000. This has become big business and anyone who is buying cattle for breeding purposes must be assured under this act that he is getting what he is paying for.
I should like to have the assurance of the Minister of Agriculture that he will consider this whole problem. We have discussed a number of other problems which in my opinion are not nearly as important as this one. We have an industry that has grown from a handful of purebred animals a year to the situation where we are now registering
130,000	such animals. This is not small business; it is a large industry in eastern Canada and it is one of the few industries in the farming field that is growing rather than going downhill. I think the government has an obligation to see that more teeth are put into this act.
We are already spending a considerable amount of money to maintain this particular division. It is doing a good job in other fields. The need is more obvious in other fields, such as compensation for the slaughtering of cattle affected with particular diseases. Obviously this is a more immediate problem and one that is seen more easily. Work has been done in this field.
We have already complimented the department and this branch of the department on the work they have done in the eradication of some of these diseases. I was pleased to note that my area was one of those that was made an area free of brucellosis. Work has been done in this field, but it seems to me that in the Live Stock Pedigree Act itself the department

was gleefully happy to obtain this foolish conviction. It is a conviction that in my opinion is more detrimental as a precedent, from their point of view, than it is advantageous. While it may have rapped this particular farmer's knuckles, it seems to me it has raised a question throughout the whole industry. I have talked to a number of farmers in the immediate area of this farmer, and they wonder why this was done. They have suggested to me that the reason it was done had no relationship to the case itself.
For this reason I think the department would be well advised to give more consideration to the technical aspects of this case. I think the department would be wise to reread the case. If they have an- expert in the department, I should like him to answer this question. Everybody knows that the gestation period of cows is the same as for human beings, nine months. I should like to know how the department is able to reconcile this fact with the fact of a calf being born within four months after the cow is supposed to have been served the second time and six months after the first service. How does the department justify this in relation to this conviction?
If they can justify it then I think we probably need some new officials and I will be happy, after they have given consideration to this question, to recommend that if it is necessary.
Shall the item carry?
Carried.

No. I hope we will hear an answer from the minister in regard to this matter. I received a letter from Mr. Rowe many months ago. Not being an expert in the field, and knowing that the hon. member for Timiskaming and his father were experts in this field, I referred the problem to my colleague the hon. member for Timiskaming.
I feel that there is a danger of bureaucracy arising in any organization, be it of lawyers, doctors, school teachers, Holstein-Friesian breeders or Yorkshire pig breeders. The moment you form an organization a vested interest is involved, and it is up to the government to ensure that the public interest is protected at all times. I believe that the case the hon. member for Timiskaming has presented is worthy of a reply.
I think you will have noted, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Timiskaming was very careful not to sit in judgment on this particular case. He was only appealing for a fair deal. This has not been assured us by the courts. The government hopes to slide out from under by not replying to the hon. member for Timiskaming. I do not think they
Supply-Agriculture
can get off that easily, and we insist upon asking the government what its intentions are in this regard.
The man who was convicted may well have been guilty, but the many problems which have arisen as a result of this conviction demand that we receive a reply and an assurance that a vested interest is not being established. We have seen vested interests established in so many other fields of Canadian life and I am sure Canadian farmers would hate to think that a vested interest was being established in any one of their particular departments. I believe the minister owes the hon. member for Timiskaming a reply on this particular case.

Mr. Chairman, I have made it very clear that I cannot deal with this particular case because it was before the courts many years ago and was settled. I can say, to make it absolutely clear to the rest of the committee, that under this act we designate to the various breeders associations the right to set the standards and enforce them. If they find people breaking these standards and trying to make false registrations of calves, they come to us and we take the action necessary under the law.
So far as the general question of the scientific aspect of it is concerned, I do not think the Department of Agriculture here in Ottawa has to yield to anyone in its constant search for ways to improve the scientific factors that go into producing pure and true breeds. I am no expert on serology which is simply a big word for the study of blood factors, but I think in their searching for new techniques for finding new ways of identifying breeds, and so on, not only in relation to cattle and horses, but poultry and every other form of livestock under this branch, the record of the department has been very good. I know it will continue to remain so.
As as as this particular case is concerned, it has been before the courts, the courts have ruled on it and I am completely helpless to say any more.

In this particular case I would quarrel with the minister and the government, not only this government but perhaps governments of the past. The minister has said that the government has granted the right to certain organizations to set standards and enforce them. To me this is most despicable, because this parliament ought to be supreme and ought not to delegate its authority to any organization.
This is what I regret in the legal profession, the medical profession and even, in this

Supp ly-A griculture
particular case, the Holstein-Friesian association. I think the public interest ought to be protected and that no legislature or parliament ought ever to forget the public interest and give to any particular vested interest the right to legislate and enforce its legislation without an appeal to the law makers of the land.
The minister has said that his department, or the government, has given these organizations the right to set standards and enforce them. I feel this is an abdication of the government's responsibility.
We enforce them.

I may have misquoted the minister and if so I apologize and hope that he will correct me but if ever the House of Commons should delegate to any other body the right to set standards where the public welfare is concerned and also the right to enforce such standards I feel we should be most negligent in our duties. If the minister has any correction to make in that regard I shall be happy to hear him.

The hon. member made one serious mistake. If I gave that impression I did not mean it. We-parliament, that is, not the government-delegate to these associations the responsibility for maintaining these standards but the enforcement is the responsibility of the only people who can enforce them, that is, the government of Canada through the law of Canada. If at any time the associations change the regulations they bring in we have to approve them.
We have to have in the working out of democracy some confidence in the professional groups of this country. What the hon. member has said today is an attack on every professional man in Canada and on every professional man and group in the democratic world. It is an attack on school teachers, dentists, lawyers, naturopaths, on any group of people organized in a professional body. Federal and provincial governments give these groups the right to set certain standards- with the approval of the government, it is true-and unless we have confidence in groups of people such as those who form these livestock associations I think the whole democratic process breaks down.
We have seen evidence tonight of this centralizing philosophy, this desire on the part of the new party to order everything under the federal government, to enforce their will upon the provinces, to enforce their will on professional associations such as these. Many of us stand here and have stood here all our lives prepared to defend the belief that parliament should have trust

in various groups of people who have come together freely in Canada to carry out their plans. There has been a clear issue put forward here today and I think the hon. member and his friends will within the next few years regret the type of remarks which have been made in the committee tonight and these violent attacks on professional associations. These breeding associations have done a good job in trying to improve the breeding characteristics of livestock here in Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That is a lot of poppycock we have heard from the minister. I did not say anything was wrong with the association though I believe they have made a number of mistakes. What I am questioning is the action or the attitude of the department itself. I do not think they are competent to give advice in this case and, incidentally, they did not give any advice in this particular case. Dr. Leslie walked around in the background prodding people but he did not get involved, and his technical advice was not used. Advice was given by the experts and those experts were all from the provincial government's veterinary college and it is certain that the federal government cannot hide behind the technical advances made by the Ontario veterinary college and say how wonderful their department is. Those experts are in Ontario; they are outstanding experts in the Ontario veterinary and agriculture college at Guelph. For the department to take credit for all that seems to me to be going very far.
I was impressed by the fact that Dr. Leslie appeared to want a conviction more than the lawyer did. I am afraid we shall have to make this case over again and let hon. members judge for themselves, telling the story as one would present a case. I had hoped the minister would give consideration to what I asked and that was not really a judgment on this particular case but that the department might be willing to go back on this case in relation to the establishment of the parentage of cattle in looking into this blood factor and making it part of the livestock act. This red factor has a great influence on the genetics of all the generations, yet the department has not seen fit to do anything about it in the form of an amendment to the act. It seems to me we are maintaining a large department with about the same record as that which looks after the Combines Investigation Act. We hear a lot of complaints but they have obtained very few convictions and this department is in the same boat. It has a lousy record. Let us not blame the Holstein-Friesian association and let us not be accused of blaming that association. They police it to the extent they are asked to police it but the department has

not put any teeth into the act or bothered to bring it up to date. The act is out of date in my opinion. No doubt it was revised in 1952 along with other acts but it is out of date in relation to the technical knowledge now available in the Ontario veterinary college.

Ten o'clock.
Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.

I wonder if the leader of the house could bring us up to date as to the government's plans for the rest of the week?

speechtext: We shall carry on tomorrow with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture followed by the estimates of the Post Office Department. Tomorrow night I will announce, if needed, another department to be considered this week if the house makes rapid progress with the agriculture estimates.
Is it understood that we go on with the estimates on Wednesday in that case?

speechtext: Yes, the intention is that on Wednesday we should carry on with the estimates. The same course will be followed on Thursday and Friday.
